ety.text: From Medieval Latin duellum (“fight between two men, duel”), itself from Old Latin duellum (“war, fight”), which survived in Classical Latin as a rare byform of bellum and was later reinterpreted as “duel” by unetymological association with duo (“two”). May have entered English through Middle French duel.

senses.d: Arranged, regular combat between two private persons, often over a matter of honor.
Historically, the wager of battle (judicial combat).
Any battle or struggle between two contending persons, forces, groups, or ideas.
ex: Apple comes out swinging in the duel of the data titans [title]
The two dogs were duelling for the bone.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish duelo, from Late Latin dolus, a derivative of Latin dolor. Compare Portuguese dó, Catalan dol, French deuil, Italian duolo.

fr:croiser le fer.gl: to cross swords (to place or hold two swords so they cross each other)

it:duellare.gl: to duel, to have or fight a duel

ety.text: From Middle English dewe, dew, due, from Old French deü (“due”), past participle of devoir (“to owe”), from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”), from dē- (“from”) + habeō (“to have”).

ex: He is due four weeks of back pay.
The amount due is just three quid.
With all due respect, you're wrong about that.
With dirges due, in sad array, / Slow through the churchway path we saw him borne.
The train is due in five minutes.

senses.d: Having reached the expected, scheduled, or natural time.
ex: The baby is just about due.

senses.d: Owing; ascribable, as to a cause.
ex: The dangerously low water table is due to rapidly growing pumping.
the milky aspect be due to a confusion of small stars

senses.d: On a direct bearing, especially for the four points of the compass.
ex: The town is 5 miles due North of the bridge.
The river runs due north for about a mile.
Give him his due – he is a good actor.

senses.d: That which is owed; debt; that which belongs or may be claimed as a right; whatever custom, law, or morality requires to be done, duty.
ex: He will give the devil his due.

For I am but an earthly Muse,
⁠And owning but a little art
⁠To lull with song an aching heart,
And render human love his dues; […]
The key of this infernal pit by due […] I keep.

6. On a direct bearing, especially for the four points of the compass
used with compass directions: directly or exactly

fr:dû.gl: what is owed, what is due, money's worth

chain.g: to owe something, to be under obligation to and for something

ety.text: Old French deü, from Vulgar Latin *dēbūtus, past participle of Latin dēbēre. Cognate to Italian dovuto. Compare dette (“debt”), from the Classical Latin past participle dēbita n pl.

Inherited from Old French plein, from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Compare Catalan ple; Italian pieno; Portuguese cheio; Romanian plin; Sardinian prenu; Spanish lleno; English plene, full.
